answer: Most Common Cause of Impotency: Anxiety. Frigidity: Sexual coldness in females.

question: The most common type of hymen is {{c1::Semilunar}}; a {{c2::Fimbriate hymen}} has natural notches often mistaken for a tear. Penile penetration causes {{c3::posterolateral}} tears, whereas digital/foreign body causes {{c4::anterior}} tears.
answer: False Virgin: Hymen remains intact even after intercourse if it is too elastic, loose, or thick (or deep-seated in a female child).

question: {{c1::Pseudocyesis (phantom/spurious pregnancy)}} occurs when a non-pregnant woman believes she is pregnant and shows amenorrhea, abdominal distension, and morning sickness, but {{c2::USG shows an empty uterus}} (Rx: counseling).
answer: Lochia (Sign of Recent Delivery): Progresses as Lochia rubra → Lochia serosa → Lochia alba.

question: {{c1::Superfecundation}} is fertilization of 2 ova from the {{c2::same ovulatory cycle}} by 2 acts of coitus (equal fetal growth / fetus papyraceus), whereas {{c3::Superfetation}} is fertilization in {{c4::different ovulatory cycles}} (unequal growth).
answer: More Terms: Supposititious child = claiming another's child as own; Atavism = resembling grandparents; Posthumous child = born after father's death; Affiliation case = fixing paternity.

question: Under the {{c1::Surrogacy Regulation Act}}, only {{c2::altruistic surrogacy}} is permitted (commercial surrogacy banned). Intending couple must be married > 5 yrs (Male 26–55, Female 23–50) with no surviving child; surrogate must be married (23–35 yrs) with {{c3::≥ 1 child of her own}}.
answer: Insurance & Limit: Surrogate eligible only once in lifetime (max 3 attempts); 3-year health insurance provided by intending couple. Unmarried couples/foreigners are NOT eligible.

question: Under the {{c1::Surrogacy Regulation Act}}, an intending woman (widow or divorcee) must be aged {{c2::35–45 years}}, and at least {{c3::one gamete}} must come from a biological parent.
answer: Not Eligible: Unmarried persons/couples and foreign nationals.

question: Under the {{c1::MTP (Amendment) Act 2021}}: {{c2::< 20 weeks}} requires 1 doctor (all indications); {{c3::20–24 weeks}} requires 2 doctors (rape/incest, minor, marital status change, disability, disaster); {{c4::> 24 weeks}} requires a Medical Board (only for substantial fetal anomaly).
answer: Records & Consent: Consent needed if > 18 yrs (guardian if < 18/mentally ill). Records preserved for 5 years (sent monthly to CMO). Criminal abortion: 88 BNS (with consent), 89 BNS (without consent), 90 BNS (resulting in death).

question: Under the MTP Act 2021, the 4-member Medical Board for termination {{c1::> 24 weeks}} comprises 1 Obstetrician, 1 Paediatrician, 1 Radiologist, and {{c2::1 independent member appointed by the State Government}}.
answer: 4 Indications for MTP: Eugenic (fetal anomaly), Therapeutic (maternal disease), Social (contraceptive failure), Humanitarian (rape).

question: Signs of intrauterine fetal death: {{c1::Maceration}} (aseptic autolysis; earliest sign is skin slippage at 12 hrs); Radiological: {{c2::Robert sign}} (gas in great vessels, 12 hrs), {{c3::Ball's sign}} (hyperflexion of spine), {{c4::Spalding sign}} (overriding cranial bones, 4–7 days).
answer: Vagitus Uterinus: Cry of baby in uterus; Vagitus Vaginalis: Cry of baby in vagina.

question: Postmortem tests for live birth (respiration): {{c1::Raygat's / Hydrostatic test}} (lung floats, Sp.Gr 0.940 vs 1.040); {{c2::Fodere's}} (lung weight 60g vs 30g); {{c3::Ploucquet's}} (1:35 vs 1:70); {{c4::Wreden's}} (middle ear clear); {{c5::Breslau's 2nd life test}} (stomach air).
answer: Diaphragm Level: 6th–7th rib if respired vs 3rd–4th rib if not respired.

question: {{c1::Battered Baby Syndrome (Caffey-Kempe syndrome)}} features discrepancy between history and injuries, multiple injuries of {{c2::varying ages}}, lower lip frenulum laceration, bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures, and {{c3::knob/string-of-beads posterior rib fractures}} on CXR.
answer: Munchausen Syndrome by Proxy: Parent fabricates illness in child and brings child to hospital to gain attention.

question: {{c1::Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS / Cot death / Crib death)}} is unexplained infant death with negative routine autopsy, except for the constant finding of {{c2::petechial hemorrhages on the heart, lungs, and thymus}}.
answer: Probable Causes: Prolonged sleep apnea, respiratory infection, hypersensitivity to cow's milk.

question: Sexual Offences under BNS/BNSS: Definition of rape = {{c1::63 BNS}}; Statutory rape age = {{c2::< 18 years}}; Mandatory free treatment = {{c3::397 BNSS}} (non-treatment punishable under 200 BNS); Victim exam = {{c4::184 BNSS}}; Accused exam = {{c5::52 BNSS}} (consent not mandatory).
answer: Punishments: 64 BNS (Rape: 10 yrs to life), 64(2) BNS (Custodial rape), 67 BNS (Separated wife), 70 BNS (Gang rape), 366(2) BNSS (In-camera trial).

question: Tests in sexual assault: {{c1::Lugol's iodine test}} on penile shaft swab (detects glycogenated vaginal epithelial cells turning brown, up to 4 days); {{c2::Toluidine blue test}} in victim detects {{c3::recent microinjuries}}.
answer: Vaginal Swab Preservation: Motile sperm seen 6–12 hrs; Sperm preserved 3 days; Semen 4 days.

question: Unnatural sexual offences: {{c1::Pederasty}} = adult male anal intercourse with child ({{c2::catamite}}); {{c3::Gerontophilia}} = with elderly; {{c4::Tribadism/Sapphism}} = between females; {{c5::Bestiality}} = with lower animals.
answer: Oral Sex: Fellatio = oral stimulation of penis; Cunnilingus = oral stimulation of vagina. Incest: Oedipus (mother-son), Electra (father-daughter), Pharaon (brother-sister).

question: Paraphilias under BNS: {{c1::Exhibitionism}} (296 BNS — streaking/mooning/flashing); {{c2::Voyeurism/Scoptophilia}} (77 BNS — Peeping Tom); {{c3::Frotteurism}} (75 BNS); {{c4::Necrophilia/Necrophagia}} (301 BNS).
answer: More Paraphilias: Sadism/Algolagnia (inflicting pain), Masochism (receiving pain), Fetishism (inanimate objects), Klismaphilia (enema), Troilism (watching spouse with another).

question: Blood stain testing: Presumptive color tests (Benzidine/Orthotoluidine = blue; Kastle-Meyer/Phenolphthalein = pink); Washed stains = {{c1::Luminol spray / UV light}}; Confirmatory = {{c2::Teichmann's}} (brown rhombic hemin crystals), {{c3::Takayama}} (pink feathery hemochromogen), and {{c4::Absorption spectrometry (most reliable)}}.
answer: Species Identification: Precipitin test (anti-human serum).

question: The {{c1::Takayama test}} is a confirmatory microchemical test for blood stains that produces {{c2::pink feathery crystals of haemochromogen}}, and is more sensitive than the Teichmann test.
answer: Teichmann's Test: Produces brown rhombic hemin crystals.

question: Seminal stain tests: {{c1::Barberio's test}} gives {{c2::yellow needle-shaped spermine picrate crystals}}; {{c3::Florence test}} gives {{c4::dark brown rhombic choline iodide crystals}}; Confirmatory = at least {{c5::1 intact spermatozoon}} on microscopy.
answer: Other Semen Tests: UV light (bluish-white fluorescence), Acid phosphatase (gives time since intercourse), P30 (PSA), CPK > 400 U.

question: The {{c1::Florence test}} for seminal stains detects choline from seminal vesicles, producing {{c2::dark brown rhombic crystals of choline iodide}}.
answer: Barberio's Test: Detects spermine from prostatic secretion (yellow needle-shaped spermine picrate crystals).

question: Hair microscopy: {{c1::Human hair}} has a narrow, fragmented or absent medulla with a {{c2::medullary index < 0.3}}, whereas {{c3::animal hair}} has a wide, continuous medulla with a {{c4::medullary index > 0.5}}.
answer: Medullary Index Formula: Diameter of medulla / Total diameter of hair shaft.

question: {{c1::Animal hair}} is microscopically distinguished from human hair by a {{c2::wider, continuous medulla}} and a medullary index {{c3::> 0.5}}.
answer: Human Hair: Fragmented/narrow medulla, medullary index < 0.3.

question: {{c1::Toxicology}} is the study of poisons, whereas {{c2::Toxinology}} is the study of {{c3::toxins (biological substances)}}. In suspected poisoning autopsies, open the {{c4::cranial cavity first}} to detect volatile odors.
answer: Legal Duties in Poisoning: Compulsory duty, preserve evidence, police intimation (33 BNSS). Failure/disappearance of evidence = 238 BNS; negligent conduct with poisons = 286 BNS.

question: Poison odors at autopsy: {{c1::Garlic}} = Arsenic, Phosphorus, Aluminium phosphide, OPC; {{c2::Bitter almond}} = Cyanide; {{c3::Burnt rope}} = Cannabis; {{c4::Acrid pear}} = Chloral hydrate (Mickey Finn); {{c5::Rotten egg}} = H₂S; {{c6::Mousy}} = Conium maculatum (Hemlock).
answer: More Odors: Hospital smell = Phenol; Kerosene = OPC; Fishy = Zinc phosphide; Fruity = Alcohol.

question: {{c1::Chloral hydrate}} (acrid pear odor) is colloquially known as {{c2::Mickey's Finn / knockout drops}} and is used as a {{c3::stupefying agent}} (often mixed with alcohol).
answer: Hemlock (Conium maculatum): Mousy odor; causes ascending paralysis.

question: Stomach mucosa appearance: {{c1::Black necrotic}} = Sulphuric acid; {{c2::Yellow}} = Nitric acid; {{c3::Buffy white leathery}} = Phenol (carbolic acid); {{c4::Bluish green}} = Copper sulphate / Sodium amytal; {{c5::Slate grey}} = Mercury; {{c6::Red velvety}} = Arsenic.
answer: Autopsy Tip: Open stomach along greater curvature after double ligation.

question: Gastric lavage (ideal < 1 hr, left lateral position) uses {{c1::Lavacuator > Ewald's tube > Ryle's tube}}. It is {{c2::absolutely contraindicated in corrosives}} (risk of perforation) {{c3::EXCEPT carbolic acid (phenol)}} (leathery mucosa).
answer: Relative Contraindications: Coma, Volatile hydrocarbons/kerosene (aspiration pneumonitis), Convulsants like Strychnine. Most rapid route of absorption: Inhalation.

question: To enhance urinary excretion of absorbed poisons: {{c1::Alkalinization (IV NaHCO₃)}} is used for {{c2::acidic drugs (salicylates, barbiturates)}}, whereas {{c3::acidification}} is rarely used for {{c4::alkaline drugs}}.
answer: Dialysis: Hemodialysis > Peritoneal dialysis; Multidose activated charcoal interrupts enterohepatic circulation.

question: Specific antidotes: {{c1::Methanol}} = Fomepizole / Ethanol; {{c2::Beta blocker}} = Glucagon; {{c3::Cyanide}} = Hydroxocobalamin (DOC) / Eli Lilly kit; {{c4::Digitalis}} = Digibind; {{c5::Acetaminophen}} = N-acetylcysteine; {{c6::Oxalic/HF/Ethylene glycol}} = IV Calcium gluconate.
answer: Contraindications of BAL (Dimercaprol) — Mnemonic IOC: Iron, Organic mercury, Cadmium. Eli Lilly Cyanide Kit: Amyl nitrite, Sodium nitrite, Sodium thiosulphate.

question: Heavy metal antidotes: {{c1::Arsenic / Mercury}} = BAL (Dimercaprol) or DMSA; {{c2::Copper}} = D-penicillamine / DMSA; {{c3::Iron}} = Desferrioxamine; {{c4::Lead (mild-mod)}} = EDTA; {{c5::Lead (severe encephalopathy)}} = EDTA + BAL/DMSA; {{c6::Cadmium}} = DMSA.
answer: Never give BAL in: Iron, Organic mercury, Cadmium (IOC).

question: Additional specific antidotes: {{c1::Cocaine}} = Amyl nitrite; {{c2::Morphine/Opioids}} = Naloxone; {{c3::Benzodiazepines}} = Flumazenil; {{c4::Organophosphates}} = Atropine + Oxime; {{c5::Carbamates}} = Atropine ONLY (no oximes); {{c6::Carbon monoxide}} = High-flow / Hyperbaric O₂.
answer: Organochlorines (Endrin, DDT) & Pyrethroids: Only supportive treatment (no specific antidote).

question: In {{c1::Barium carbonate (rat poison)}} poisoning (white, odorless powder), the hallmark electrolyte abnormality is profound {{c2::hypokalemia (↓ K⁺)}} leading to flaccid paralysis.
answer: Mechanism: Barium blocks potassium efflux channels causing intracellular K⁺ trapping.

question: Corrosives: {{c1::Acids}} cause {{c2::coagulative necrosis}} (EXCEPT {{c3::Hydrofluoric acid}} → liquefactive necrosis), whereas {{c4::Alkalis}} cause {{c5::liquefactive necrosis}} (more dangerous due to deep lateral spread).
answer: Inorganic Acids (local only): H₂SO₄, HNO₃, HCl. Organic Acids (local + systemic): Carbolic, Oxalic, Acetic.

question: {{c1::Sulphuric acid (Oil of Vitriol)}} causes {{c2::carbonization}} (black necrotic tongue & stomach, black charred skin) and {{c3::chalky white teeth}} (hygroscopic action), whereas {{c4::Nitric acid}} produces {{c5::yellow discoloration (picric acid / xanthoproteic reaction)}}.
answer: Vitriolage (Acid Attack): Punishable under Section 124 BNS; mandatory free treatment under 397 BNSS.

question: {{c1::Carbolic acid (Phenol)}} is absorbed by all routes, delays putrefaction, turns stomach mucosa {{c2::buffy white & leathery}}, and is metabolized to pyrocatechol/hydroquinone causing {{c3::olive-green urine (carboluria)}} and {{c4::ochronosis}}.
answer: Gastric Lavage Exception: Phenol is the ONLY corrosive where cautious gastric lavage can be performed.

question: {{c1::Oxalic acid}} (acid of sugar / ink stain remover) chelates serum calcium causing {{c2::hypocalcemic tetany}} and excretes {{c3::dumbbell / postal-envelope shaped calcium oxalate crystals}} in urine (oxaluria).
answer: Antidote: IV Calcium gluconate. Avoid gastric lavage if severe corrosion.

question: Most common acute heavy metal poisoning is {{c1::Arsenic}}; most common chronic heavy metal poisoning is {{c2::Lead}} (children: oral; adults: occupational inhalation).
answer: Arsenic Most Toxic Form: Arsine gas; Most Toxic Salt: Arsenic trioxide.

question: Chronic {{c1::Arsenic poisoning (Arsenicosis)}} features (Mnemonic ARSENIC): {{c2::Aldrich-Mees lines}} (transverse white nail bands), Alopecia, {{c3::Raindrop pigmentation}}, Palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, Symmetrical sensory-motor neuropathy (mimics GBS), and {{c4::Blackfoot disease}}.
answer: Acute Arsenic: Cholera-like rice-water purging + red velvety stomach mucosa. Tests: Marsh test, Reinsch test, NAA, AAS. Detected even in cremated/exhumed remains.

question: {{c1::Raindrop pigmentation}} (dappled hyper- and hypopigmentation) with palmoplantar hyperkeratosis is characteristic of chronic {{c2::arsenic}} poisoning (often from contaminated groundwater / hydroarsenicism).
answer: Tests: Marsh test, Reinsch test, NAA, AAS.

question: Samples for Arsenic poisoning: Acute = {{c1::Urine (most reliable) > Blood}}; Chronic = {{c2::Bone, nail, hair}}. It can be detected in {{c3::exhumed, decomposed, and cremated remains}}.
answer: Soil Sample at Exhumation: Collected to rule out postmortem imbibition of Arsenic.

question: Chronic {{c1::Mercury poisoning (Hydrargyrism)}} (Mnemonic METAL): {{c2::Minamata disease}} (methyl Hg in fish), {{c3::Erethism}} (mad hatter syndrome), Intentional {{c4::Tremors}} (hatter's shakes), {{c5::Acrodynia (Pink disease)}}, and Mercuria {{c6::lentis}}.
answer: Elemental Mercury: Non-toxic if swallowed orally, but toxic if inhaled as vapor. Organic (methyl Hg) > Inorganic toxicity.

question: In {{c1::Lead poisoning}}, organic {{c2::tetraethyl lead}} crosses the BBB causing encephalopathy, whereas among inorganic forms {{c3::lead tetroxide}} is most toxic, {{c4::lead carbonate}} is in paints, and {{c5::lead sulphide}} is least toxic.
answer: Mnemonic ABCDEFG for Plumbism: Anemia, Basophilic stippling, Burtonian/Bone line, Colic, Cabot ring, Drop (wrist/foot), Encephalopathy, Facial pallor, Gout.

question: Chronic {{c1::Lead poisoning (Plumbism / Saturnism)}} inhibits ALA dehydratase & ferrochelatase (microcytic anemia) and {{c2::5'-pyrimidine nucleotidase}} causing {{c3::basophilic stippling of RBCs}}.
answer: Screen Workers: Urinary ALA ↑↑. Blood Tests: Free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP) and Zinc protoporphyrin (ZPP). Most consistent sign: Facial pallor.

question: In chronic lead poisoning, blue-black stippled deposition on the gingival margin of carious teeth is called {{c1::Burtonian line}}, and dense radiopaque metaphyseal bands in children are called {{c2::lead bone lines}}.
answer: Other Metals Causing Blue Gum Lines (Blue SIM Card): Bismuth, Silver, Iron, Mercury, Copper. Also seen: Wrist/foot drop, Painter's colic, Saturnine gout.

question: Radiopaque {{c1::metaphyseal dense bands (lead bone lines)}} on knee/wrist X-rays in a child with microcytic anemia and abdominal colic indicate chronic {{c2::lead poisoning}}.
answer: Antidote: Mild-moderate = EDTA; Severe (with encephalopathy) = EDTA + BAL/DMSA.

question: {{c1::Cadmium}} causes {{c2::Itai-itai (Ouch-ouch) disease}} (yellow teeth ring + osteomalacia/pathological fractures). {{c3::Thallium}} causes {{c4::alopecia with madarosis}} (loss of eyebrows — NOT seen in arsenic), Aldrich-Mees lines, and neuropathy (Rx: {{c5::Prussian blue}}).
answer: High-Yield Differentiation: Both Arsenic and Thallium cause Mees lines and GBS-like neuropathy, but madarosis is unique to Thallium!

question: {{c1::White phosphorus}} (toxic, luminous, garlic odor) causes acute {{c2::smoky stool syndrome}} (3 stages: GI → asymptomatic → hepatic failure) and chronic {{c3::Phossy jaw (osteonecrosis of mandible)}}. Topical burn Rx: {{c4::CuSO₄}}.
answer: Red Phosphorus: Non-toxic (used on matchbox striking surfaces). Aluminium Phosphide (Celphos): Releases phosphine gas; silver nitrate breath test turns black; no antidote (supportive + MgSO₄).

question: In acute {{c1::white phosphorus}} poisoning, Stage 1 features luminescent vomitus/stool ({{c2::smoky stool syndrome}}), followed by an {{c3::asymptomatic Stage 2}} (discharging patient = medical negligence) before fatal Stage 3 hepatic/multiorgan failure.
answer: Phosphorus Burn First Aid: Topical CuSO₄ precipitates copper phosphide preventing further combustion.

question: {{c1::Aluminium phosphide (Celphos)}} tablets release {{c2::phosphine gas}} on contact with gastric HCl. Diagnosis is by {{c3::silver nitrate breath test (filter paper turns black)}}; management is supportive + {{c4::MgSO₄}}.
answer: Antidote: No specific antidote exists.

question: Toxic plants: {{c1::Ricinus communis}} (Ricin — inhibits protein synthesis; residue toxic, oil non-toxic); {{c2::Abrus precatorius}} (Abrin — powdered seeds form {{c3::Sui needles}} mimicking viperine cattle bite).
answer: Croton tiglium (Jamal gota): Both oil and residue toxic (Crotin). Calotropis (Madar): All parts toxic (Calotropin). Capsicum annum: Hunan's hand syndrome.

question: In {{c1::Ricinus communis (Castor)}} seeds, the extracted oil is {{c2::non-toxic}} while the residue contains {{c3::Ricin}} (inhibits protein synthesis causing bloody diarrhea); in {{c4::Croton tiglium (Jamal gota)}}, BOTH oil and residue are toxic.
answer: Calotropis (Madar/Akdo): All parts are toxic (Calotropin, Calotoxin, Calactin).

question: {{c1::Semecarpus anacardium (Marking nut / Bhilawa)}} produces a black juice (Bhilawanol) used for malingering to create {{c2::artificial bruises}} with blisters and intense itching.
answer: Capsicum annum: Active principles Capsicin/Capsaicin cause Hunan's hand syndrome (occupational contact dermatitis).

question: {{c1::Papaver somniferum (Opium)}} yields morphine and codeine from dried milky capsule exudate (its {{c2::seeds are non-toxic}}). Heroin is {{c3::diacetylmorphine}}; triad of toxicity = {{c4::coma, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression}} (Rx: {{c5::Naloxone}}).
answer: Heroin Abuse Routes: Chasing the dragon (inhaling vapor), Mainlining (IV), Skin popping (SC).

question: {{c1::Datura}} (Deliriants Mnemonic CCD: Cocaine, Cannabis, Datura) contains {{c2::hyoscine, hyoscyamine, atropine}} (anticholinergic: dilated pupils, dry secretions, muttering delirium). Used as a {{c3::railway/roadside stupefying poison}}; antidote = {{c4::Physostigmine}}.
answer: Most Toxic Parts: Roots and seeds.

question: Differentiating {{c1::Datura seeds}} from {{c2::Chilli seeds}}: Datura seeds are {{c3::dark brown, thick, rough, kidney-shaped, and odorless}}, whereas Chilli seeds are {{c4::yellow, thin, smooth, oval-shaped, with pungent smell}}.
answer: Fruit Comparison: Datura fruit (thorn apple) is single & large; Castor fruit is small & in clusters.

question: In {{c1::Cannabis sativa}} (active principle: {{c2::THC}}), potency order is: Bhang (dried leaves <15%) < Ganja (female flower 15–25%) < Charas/Hashish (25–40%) < {{c3::Hash oil (60–70%)}}.
answer: Chronic Cannabis Syndromes (AIR): Amotivational syndrome, Hashish insanity, Run amok (homicidal impulse — not liable under 22 BNS), Koro phenomenon, Flashback phenomenon.

question: In {{c1::Body Packer Syndrome}} (swallowed cocaine/heroin packets seen on abdominal X-ray): if packs are intact/asymptomatic → {{c2::whole bowel irrigation with PEG}}; if ruptured (cocaine) → acute sympathomimetic toxicity (antidote: {{c3::Amyl nitrite}}).
answer: Chronic Cocaine Triad: Black staining of tongue/teeth, Nasal septal perforation, Peripheral gangrene. Tactile hallucinations = Magnan's syndrome (cocaine bugs / formication).

question: Order of alcohol toxicity: {{c1::Isopropyl alcohol > Methanol > Ethanol}}. Ethanol absorption occurs {{c2::20% in stomach and 80% in small intestine}}, and {{c3::alcoholic gaze nystagmus}} appears at {{c4::80–100 mg% BAC}}.
answer: Legal Driving Limit in India: 30 mg% BAC (Section 185 Motor Vehicles Act). Effect is greater in females (smaller total body water).

question: Ethanol compartment ratios: Blood : Urine = {{c1::1 : 1.3}}; Blood : CSF = {{c2::1 : 1.1}}; Blood : Vitreous = {{c3::1 : 1.2}}; Blood : Alveolar air = {{c4::1 : 2100}} (used in breath analyzers).
answer: Withdrawal Syndromes: 6–12h = Abstinence/Tremors; 12–24h = Hallucinosis; 24–48h = Rum fits; 2–5d = Delirium tremens (not criminally liable under 22 BNS).

question: Alcohol-induced thiamine deficiency causes {{c1::Wernicke's encephalopathy}} (triad Mnemonic {{c2::GOA}}: Global confusion, Ophthalmoplegia, Ataxia) and {{c3::Korsakoff's syndrome}} (memory impairment + {{c4::confabulation}}).
answer: Methanol Poisoning: Metabolized via ADH/ALDH to formaldehyde & formic acid → retinal/optic nerve blindness + HAGMA (mass poisoning = Hooch tragedy).

question: {{c1::Ethylene glycol}} (antifreeze solution) is metabolized to glycolic acid and {{c2::oxalic acid}}, causing {{c3::HAGMA, hypocalcemia, and calcium oxalate crystalluria}}.
answer: Antidote: Fomepizole / Ethanol + IV Calcium gluconate.

question: {{c1::Strychnos nux vomica (Kuchila)}} blocks postsynaptic {{c2::glycine}} at spinal anterior horn cells, causing {{c3::opisthotonus}} (most common backward arch), {{c4::risus sardonicus}}, early rigor mortis, postmortem caloricity, and delayed putrefaction.
answer: Fatal Dose: Even 1 crushed seed is fatal (whole seeds pass unabsorbed). Consciousness remains clear until death.

question: The spastic grinning facial expression with retracted mouth angles seen in strychnine poisoning (and tetanus) is called {{c1::Risus sardonicus}}.
answer: Autopsy Note: Spinal cord (full length) via posterior approach is preserved in strychnine fatalities.

question: Cardiac poisons (Mnemonic {{c1::Car DONA}}: Digitalis, Oleander, Nicotine, Aconite): {{c2::Aconite (Mitha zaher / Monk's hood)}} has its highest toxicity in the {{c3::root}} and causes perioral paresthesia, arrhythmias, and {{c4::Hippus}} (alternating pupil constriction/dilation).
answer: Other Cardiotoxic Plants: Pink oleander (Nerium odorum), Yellow oleander (Cerbera thevetia), Suicide tree (Cerbera odollam — confused with mango), Foxglove (Digitalis — Rx: Digibind).

question: Identify these cardiotoxic plants: {{c1::Cerbera odollam}} (fruit confused with mango → accidental poisoning), {{c2::Cerbera thevetia}} (Yellow oleander: Thevetin, Cerberin), {{c3::Nerium odorum}} (Pink oleander: Neriodorin, Karabin), {{c4::Digitalis}} (Foxglove → Rx Digibind).
answer: Mechanism: Inhibit Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase causing lethal cardiac arrhythmias and hyperkalemia.

question: {{c1::Carbon monoxide (CO)}} has {{c2::210 times}} higher affinity for hemoglobin than O₂, shifting the ODC to the {{c3::left}} (anemic anoxia) and producing {{c4::cherry-red skin/hypostasis}}, cutaneous blisters, and {{c5::B/L symmetrical necrosis of lenticular nucleus}}.
answer: Treatment: Moderate = High-flow O₂; Severe = Hyperbaric O₂ (risk of barotrauma). Cutaneous blisters at autopsy = CO and Barbiturate poisoning.

question: At {{c1::40–50% COHb}}, CO poisoning causes confusion, ataxia, motor incoordination (mimicking drunkenness), and cherry-red skin; {{c2::50–70%}} causes coma; {{c3::> 80%}} causes rapid respiratory arrest.
answer: Myoglobin Binding: Causes rebound toxicity after initial recovery.

question: {{c1::Cyanide}} (bitter almond odor) and {{c2::H₂S}} (rotten egg odor) both inhibit {{c3::cytochrome oxidase (ETC)}} causing {{c4::histotoxic anoxia}} and lactic acidosis; Cyanide gives {{c5::brick-red}} hypostasis while H₂S gives {{c6::bluish-green}} hypostasis.
answer: Methyl Isocyanate (MIC): Most common irritant asphyxiant gas (Bhopal Gas Tragedy).

question: {{c1::Argemone mexicana}} (yellow/Mexican poppy) adulterates mustard oil; its active principles {{c2::sanguinarine and dihydrosanguinarine}} cause {{c3::Epidemic dropsy}} (bilateral pitting edema, glaucoma, high-output cardiac failure).
answer: Screening Tests for Argemone: Nitric acid test (orange-red) and Paper chromatography.

question: Venomous snakes have {{c1::large belly scales covering the entire breadth}} of the belly, compressed tail, 2 fang marks, and are nocturnal. {{c2::Cobra}} has largest 3rd supralabial scale; {{c3::Krait}} has largest 4th infralabial scale.
answer: 3 Venomous Families: Elapidae (Neurotoxic: Cobra, Krait), Viperidae (Hemotoxic: Russell's, Saw-scaled), Hydrophidae (Myotoxic: Sea snake → hyperkalemia/tall T waves).

question: Among the 'Big 4' venomous snakes of India: {{c1::Common Krait (Bungarus caeruleus)}} has the lowest fatal dose ({{c2::6 mg}}), {{c3::King Cobra (Ophiophagus hannah)}} is the longest venomous snake (fatal dose 12 mg), and {{c4::Russell's viper}} shows 3 rows of diamond spots.
answer: Sea Snake (Hydrophidae): Myotoxic venom causing myonecrosis, renal failure, and hyperkalemia (tall T waves).

question: In {{c1::Elapidae (Cobra/Krait)}} bites, the earliest neurotoxic sign is {{c2::ptosis}}, progressing to descending paralysis and {{c3::respiratory failure}}; monitored via {{c4::Single Breath Count Test}} and treated with ASV + {{c5::IV Neostigmine + Atropine}} (for Cobra).
answer: First Aid (RIGHT): Reassure, Immobilize limb with crepe bandage (55–70 mmHg to occlude lymphatics — NEVER tourniquet/incision), Get to hospital, Tell symptoms.

question: In {{c1::Viperidae (Russell's / Saw-scaled viper)}} bites, hemotoxic venom causes {{c2::DIC and spontaneous bleeding}}, diagnosed bedside by the {{c3::20-minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (WBCT)}} (no clot after 20 mins).
answer: Big 4 Snakes Covered by Polyvalent ASV: Common cobra, Common krait, Russell's viper, Saw-scaled viper (IV 8–10 vials).

question: {{c1::Indian Red Scorpion}} envenomation leaves a single puncture mark and triggers an {{c2::autonomic storm}} (cholinergic + adrenergic → pulmonary edema, myocarditis); drug of choice is {{c3::Prazosin}} (+ anti-scorpion venom).
answer: Spanish Fly (Cantharides): Active principle Cantharidin; used as aphrodisiac; causes skin blisters, hematuria, nephrotoxicity, and priapism.

question: {{c1::Spanish fly (Cantharides)}} contains {{c2::cantharidin}}, is used in powdered form as an aphrodisiac, and causes local blistering, hematuria, {{c3::nephrotoxicity}}, and {{c4::priapism}}.
answer: Management: Avoid oily demulcents (increase cantharidin absorption).

question: {{c1::Organophosphorus (OP) poisoning}} causes irreversible AChE inhibition: Acute cholinergic crisis (<24h: {{c2::DUMBELS}} muscarinic → Rx {{c3::Atropine}}; nicotinic → Rx {{c4::Oximes}}); {{c5::Intermediate syndrome (1–4 days)}}; {{c6::Delayed neuropathy (1–4 weeks)}}.
answer: Labs: RBC cholinesterase (most specific) vs Pseudocholinesterase (most sensitive). Stop atropine when airway secretions are dried and clear (atropinisation).

question: Delusions: {{c1::Othello syndrome}} = infidelity of spouse; {{c2::De Clerambault syndrome (Erotomania)}} = superior person is in love with patient; {{c3::Capgras syndrome}} = double has replaced close relative; {{c4::Fregoli syndrome}} = familiar person disguises as strangers.
answer: Nihilistic Delusion: Patient believes they/world do not exist (seen in severe depression). Grandeur / Persecution / Reference / Influence: Common in schizophrenia.

question: {{c1::Hallucination}} is a false sense of perception {{c2::without external stimuli}} (e.g., tactile hallucination = {{c3::Magnan's syndrome}} in cocaine abuse), whereas {{c4::Illusion}} is a false interpretation of an existing external stimulus.
answer: Hypochondriacal Delusion: Medically fit person repeatedly visits hospital believing they have a serious illness.

question: Impulse disorders: {{c1::Kleptomania}} = stealing items of low value; {{c2::Pyromania}} = setting fires; {{c3::Trichotillomania}} = pulling own hair; {{c4::Dipsomania}} = irresistible drinking; {{c5::Oniomania}} = compulsive shopping.
answer: Phobias: Acrophobia (heights), Agoraphobia (crowds/open spaces), Claustrophobia (closed spaces), Nyctophobia (darkness), Mysophobia (germs).

question: In forensic psychiatry, a {{c1::lucid interval}} is a period of sanity between episodes of mental illness; {{c2::testamentary capacity}} is the ability to make a valid will ({{c3::holographic will}} = handwritten by self).
answer: Onus of Proof of Insanity: Law presumes everyone is sane; burden of proving unsoundness of mind lies on the accused. Psychiatric evaluation = 367 BNSS.

question: Criminal responsibility of the insane: {{c1::Section 22 BNS}} (adapted from {{c2::McNaughten's rule / Right-Wrong test}}) states an act is not an offence if the person was incapable of knowing the {{c3::nature of the act}} or that it was {{c4::wrong/contrary to law}}.
answer: Other Rules: Durham's rule ('product of mental disease'), Curren's rule (capacity to regulate conduct), Irresistible Impulse Act (New Hampshire doctrine), ALI Act.

question: Insanity legal tests: {{c1::Durham's rule}} = act is a product of mental disease/defect; {{c2::Curren's rule}} = lacked capacity to regulate conduct; {{c3::Irresistible impulse (New Hampshire doctrine)}} = knew nature of act but incapable of restraining self.
answer: ALI (American Law Institute) Act: Lacks adequate capacity to appreciate the criminality of the act.

question: Age & intoxication criminal liability under BNS: {{c1::< 7 years (20 BNS)}} = never liable; {{c2::7–12 years (21 BNS)}} = liable if mentally mature; {{c3::Insane (22 BNS)}} = not liable; {{c4::Involuntary drunkenness (23 BNS)}} = not liable; {{c5::Voluntary drunkenness (24 BNS)}} = liable.
answer: Injury Definition (Section 2(14) BNS): Any harm illegally caused to Body, Mind, Reputation, or Property.

question: Male offences against women under BNS: {{c1::74 BNS}} = Indecent assault (outraging modesty); {{c2::75 BNS}} = Sexual harassment; {{c3::76 BNS}} = Using force to disrobe; {{c4::77 BNS}} = Voyeurism; {{c5::78 BNS}} = Stalking; {{c6::80 BNS}} = Dowry death (<7 yrs marriage).
answer: Rape Victim Identity Protection: Section 72 BNS prohibits disclosure of rape victim's identity.

question: Key BNS Legal Sections: {{c1::100 BNS}} = Culpable homicide; {{c2::103 BNS}} = Murder; {{c3::106(1) BNS}} = Death due to medical negligence; {{c4::108 BNS}} = Abetment of suicide; {{c5::238 BNS}} = Disappearance of evidence; {{c6::124 BNS}} = Vitriolage (acid attack).
answer: Infectious Spread: 271 BNS = Negligent act spreading fatal infection; 272 BNS = Malignant/intentional act spreading fatal infection.

question: Hurt sections under BNS: {{c1::114 BNS}} = Definition of hurt; {{c2::115 BNS}} = Voluntarily causing hurt; {{c3::116 BNS}} = Definition of grievous hurt; {{c4::117 BNS}} = Voluntarily causing grievous hurt; {{c5::118(1)/(2) BNS}} = Hurt/grievous hurt with dangerous weapon.
answer: Consent in Emergency: Section 30 BNS (emergency life-saving treatment without consent is protected).

question: The 8 clauses of {{c1::Grievous Hurt (Section 116 BNS)}} include: Emasculation, Permanent privation of eye/ear/member/joint, Permanent disfiguration of head/face, Fracture/dislocation of bone/tooth, and hurt endangering life or causing disability for {{c2::15 days}}.
answer: BNS Update Note: Under old IPC 320 it was 20 days; under 116 BNS it is 15 days!

question: Under the {{c1::Transplantation of Human Organs Act (THOA 1994/2014)}}, brainstem death is certified by a 4-member medical board (Treating doctor, Hospital RMP in-charge, Independent RMP, Neurologist/Neurosurgeon) tested twice {{c2::6 hours apart}}; the {{c3::transplant surgeon}} is NEVER on the team.
answer: Unclaimed Bodies: Hospital management can authorize organ harvesting after 48 hours. Eye donation does not require a registered hospital.

question: Brainstem death criteria under THOA require: (1) Ruling out {{c1::reversible causes (hypothermia, electrolyte imbalance, poisoning)}}, (2) Confirming {{c2::irreversible coma}}, (3) {{c3::Absence of cranial reflexes}}, and (4) Positive {{c4::apnea test}}.
answer: Violation Penalty: Doctor involved in illegal organ trade faces penal erasure by State Medical Council.

question: Under the {{c1::POCSO Act 2012}} (protects any child {{c2::< 18 years}} irrespective of gender): mandatory police reporting is required, medical exam follows {{c3::184 BNSS}}, and a girl child can be examined ONLY by a {{c4::female doctor}}.
answer: Aggravated PSA/SA (Mnemonic TRAIT): Person of Trust, Repeat offender, Age < 12 years, Insane victim, Two or more people (gang).

question: POCSO Act 2012 classifies offences into: {{c1::Penetrative Sexual Assault (PSA)}} (penetration/mouth to vagina, mouth, urethra, anus), {{c2::Sexual Assault (SA)}} (touching private parts / hormones for early maturity), {{c3::Sexual Harassment}}, and {{c4::Pornography}}.
answer: Exam Requirement: Conducted in the presence of parent, guardian, or any person of trust.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A body recovered from a fire shows soot in the trachea, COHb of 25%, and sparing of skin folds around the lateral angles of the eyes. What is this external finding called? {{c1::Crow feet sign (indicates antemortem burn)}}.
answer: Exam Pearl: Crow feet sign + soot in lower airways + elevated COHb (> 10%) prove the victim was alive and squinting/breathing during the fire.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] In a road traffic accident, a front-seat passenger sustains multiple small angular cut lacerations on the face from shattered tempered windshield glass. These are classically known as {{c1::Sparrow foot mark injuries}}.
answer: Mechanism: Tempered windshield glass shatters into small cuboidal/angular fragments causing characteristic 'sparrow-foot' lacerations.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] A bruise over the injured thigh appears brown on examination. What is the approximate age of this contusion and the pigment responsible? {{c1::Day 4; Hemosiderin}}.
answer: Bruise Aging Sequence: Fresh = Red (OxyHb); Few hrs–3d = Blue (DeoxyHb); Day 4 = Brown (Hemosiderin); Day 5–6 = Green (Biliverdin); Day 7–12 = Yellow (Bilirubin).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A bruise appears greenish in color at its periphery. What is the approximate age of the contusion and the pigment responsible? {{c1::5–6 days; Biliverdin}}.
answer: Pearl: Color changes always progress from periphery to center; yellow (Bilirubin) appears at 7–12 days.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Why does a subconjunctival hemorrhage NOT undergo the typical color changes of a cutaneous bruise? {{c1::Direct diffusion of atmospheric oxygen keeps hemoglobin oxygenated (bright red)}}.
answer: Contrast: Cutaneous bruises change Red → Blue → Brown → Green → Yellow.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] An abrasion shows a heaped-up epithelial tag at one end. What does the epithelial tag indicate? {{c1::Tail end of the abrasion and direction of force}}.
answer: Aging (R³B³): Raw (<12h) → Reddish (>12h) → Reddish-brown (2–3d) → Brown (4–5d) → Black (6–7d).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A pedestrian is struck by a car and sustains a bumper fracture of the tibia. Which impact phase does this represent? {{c1::Primary impact injury}}.
answer: Phases: 1st impact with vehicle = Primary impact; 2nd impact with vehicle = Secondary impact; Ground impact = Tertiary impact / Secondary injuries.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A patient with head trauma develops ecchymosis behind the ear over the mastoid process 36 hours after injury. Name the sign and underlying fracture: {{c1::Battle sign; Middle cranial fossa fracture}}.
answer: Black Eye Sign: Ectopic bruise from forehead trauma or anterior cranial fossa fracture.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] A linear wound over the eyebrow caused by a blunt iron rod has clean-looking margins, mimicking an incised wound. How do you confirm it is a split laceration? {{c1::Presence of crushed hair bulbs and intact tissue bridges in the depth}}.
answer: Common Sites: Scalp, eyebrows, cheekbone, and shin (where skin overlies bone).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Multiple parallel superficial linear cuts on the volar aspect of the left wrist of a right-handed individual are known as {{c1::Hesitation (tentative) cuts, indicating suicide}}.
answer: Contrast: Deep cuts on palms/1st web space = Active defence cuts (homicide).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A victim has deep incised wounds across the palmar aspect of the fingers and 1st web space. What do these represent? {{c1::Active defence cuts (homicide — attempting to grasp the blade)}}.
answer: Passive Defence Cuts: On extensor/ulnar forearm and wrist.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] A stab wound is wedge-shaped with one acute angle and one blunt angle showing fish-tailing. What weapon caused it? {{c1::Single-edged knife}}.
answer: Double-edged Knife: Produces an elliptical/spindle wound with both ends acute.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Why does a stab wound oriented perpendicular to Langer's lines gape widely compared to one parallel to them? {{c1::Cut collagen fibers retract maximally when transected perpendicularly}}.
answer: Langer's Lines: Represent orientation of dermal collagen fibers.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A charred body recovered from a house fire exhibits flexion at elbows, knees, and hips ('boxer's / pugilistic attitude'). Does this prove antemortem burning? {{c1::No — it is a non-specific heat artefact from protein coagulation > 65°C}}.
answer: Specific Signs of Antemortem Burns: Soot in airway, ↑ COHb (>10%), Crow feet sign, vital reaction in blister base.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] At autopsy of a charred body, a chocolate-brown, honeycomb-appearing blood clot is found in the extradural space. What is it? {{c1::Heat hematoma (postmortem artefact)}}.
answer: Differentiation from Antemortem EDH: Heat hematoma is bilateral/diffuse, honeycomb, chocolate-brown, and lacks skull fracture at pterion.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which chart is the BEST for estimating burn surface area in young children? {{c1::Lund and Browder chart}}.
answer: Wallace Rule of 9s in Child: Head & neck = 18%, each lower limb = 13.5%.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A person struck by lightning develops fern-like, branching erythematous markings on the chest. Name this finding: {{c1::Filigree burns (Lichtenberg / Arborescent / Keraunographic markings)}}.
answer: Electrocution Joule Burn: Low-voltage firm contact produces central depressed crater with raised pale margins.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] In an air blast explosion, which organ is MOST COMMONLY injured and which is MOST FATAL in primary blast injury? {{c1::Ear (tympanic membrane) is most common; Lung (blast lung) is most fatal}}.
answer: Secondary Air Blast: Most common overall (flying missiles → Marshal's triad).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A torture victim is suspended by wrists tied behind the back. What is this method called? {{c1::Strappado (Palestinian hanging / La bandera)}}.
answer: Parrot's Perch: Wrists and ankles tied over a horizontal pole; Falanga: Beating soles of feet.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A patient with head trauma has a brief loss of consciousness, recovers completely (lucid interval), and then deteriorates into coma. CT shows a biconvex hyperdensity that does not cross sutures. Diagnosis & vessel? {{c1::Extradural hemorrhage (EDH); Middle meningeal artery}}.
answer: Autopsy Note: Missing a lucid interval leading to death is medical negligence under 106(1) BNS.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] At autopsy, how do you differentiate Subdural Hemorrhage (SDH) from Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) by pouring water? {{c1::SDH clears/washes away after pouring water, whereas SAH remains intact}}.
answer: CT Appearance: SDH = Crescentic (crosses sutures); EDH = Biconvex (respects sutures).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A skull fracture shows two linear fracture lines where Line B terminates abruptly at Line A. According to Puppe's rule, which blow occurred first? {{c1::Line A (the continuous line) occurred first; Line B occurred second}}.
answer: Puppe's Rule: A newer fracture line will never cross an already existing fracture line.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A motorcyclist sustains a fatal side-impact head collision resulting in a transverse fracture running across the middle cranial fossa from one temporal bone to the other. This is called {{c1::Type I hinge fracture (Motorcyclist fracture)}}.
answer: Ring Fracture: Encircles foramen magnum (fall from height landing on feet/buttocks).

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] A 2-year-old child falls from a bed and develops an indented, ping-pong ball-like depression on the parietal bone without a fracture line. This is a {{c1::Pond fracture (Ping-pong fracture)}}.
answer: Mechanism: Seen exclusively in soft, pliable infant/child skulls (< 4 years).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which is the MOST COMMON site of contrecoup injury following an occipital impact (fall backward hitting occiput)? {{c1::Frontal lobe (inferior/anterior surface)}}.
answer: Frontal Impact: Produces little or no contrecoup injury.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A fall from height landing on the feet or buttocks drives the spine into the skull base, producing a {{c1::Ring fracture around the foramen magnum}}.
answer: Depressed Signature Fracture: Caused by hammer/small striking surface.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A gunshot wound on the skull shows punched-out outer table and bevelling of the inner table. Which wound is this? {{c1::Entry wound}}.
answer: Rule of Skull Bevelling: Bevelling always faces the direction of bullet travel — Inner table bevel = Entry; Outer table bevel = Exit.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A victim of a tight contact rifle shot over the forehead has a cruciate/stellate wound with EVERTED margins and soot inside the track. Why are the margins everted? {{c1::Blast effect / Blowback phenomenon of expanding gases against underlying bone}}.
answer: Trap: Distant entry wounds have inverted margins; tight contact over bone is the classic exception with everted margins.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] Which collar around a bullet entry wound is diagnostic of an entry wound (caused by lubricant/soot wiping off the bullet), and which outer collar gives trajectory? {{c1::Grease collar (inner); Abrasion collar (outer)}}.
answer: Eccentric Abrasion Collar: Points toward the side from which the bullet entered.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] What is the specific test of choice for Gunshot Residue (GSR) detection from swabs of the firing hand? {{c1::SEM-EDXA (Scanning Electron Microscopy with Energy Dispersive X-ray Analysis)}}.
answer: Mnemonic HANDS: Harrison-Gilroy, AAS, Neutron activation, Dermal nitrate (paraffin), SEM-EDXA.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] In shotgun injuries, a central entry hole surrounded by independent satellite pellet holes indicates which range? {{c1::Intermediate / Medium range (2–4 meters)}}.
answer: Near Shot (1–2 m): Scalloped/rat-hole margins; Distant Shot (> 4 m): Complete dispersion with independent pellet holes.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] How is the caliber of a rifled firearm measured? {{c1::Distance between two diametrically opposite lands}}.
answer: Shotgun Gauge: Number of spherical lead balls made from 1 pound of lead that precisely fit the barrel.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which firearm is a smooth-bored shotgun that has rifling in the terminal few inches of its barrel? {{c1::Paradox gun}}.
answer: Choking: Narrowing terminal end of shotgun barrel to reduce dispersion (Full choke = least dispersion).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] What is the composition of black gunpowder? {{c1::Potassium nitrate (75%), Charcoal (15%), and Sulphur (10%)}}.
answer: Smokeless Gunpowder: Nitrocellulose (single base), + Nitroglycerine (double), + Nitroguanidine (triple).

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] What is the Kennedy phenomenon in forensic ballistics? {{c1::Iatrogenic surgical alteration/suturing of a gunshot wound causing difficulty in range and entry/exit determination}}.
answer: Ricochet Bullet: Keyhole entry wound with no abrasion collar.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A retained 'souvenir bullet' inside the body becomes surrounded by fibrous tissue and can cause which long-term complication? {{c1::Chronic lead poisoning (Plumbism / Saturnism)}}.
answer: Handling Bullet at Autopsy: Use rubber-tipped tweezers and gloved hands.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A dead body shows greenish-brown branching arborization of superficial veins over the chest and shoulders. What is this putrefactive sign, its pigment, and time since death? {{c1::Marbling; Sulfhemoglobin; 36–72 hours}}.
answer: Pathogenesis: Bacterial H₂S reacts with hemoglobin in superficial veins forming sulfhemoglobin.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which is the FIRST external sign of putrefaction and where does it appear? {{c1::Greenish discoloration in the right iliac fossa}} (12–18 hrs in summer, 1–2 days in winter).
answer: Reason: Cecum lies superficially in the RIF and contains abundant gas/bacteria (Clostridium welchii). First internal sign = Aorta.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] A decomposed body recovered from warm, moist, stagnant water shows a greyish-white, greasy, waxy substance with a sweet rancid odor on the cheeks and thighs. Identify the process and minimum duration: {{c1::Adipocere (Saponification); 3 weeks to 3 months}}.
answer: Mechanism: Hydrolysis and hydrogenation of subcutaneous fat by Clostridium welchii lecithinase.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which autopsy incision is MANDATORY in custodial deaths and why? {{c1::X-shaped incision}} (from shoulders to iliac crests on posterior aspect to expose deep subcutaneous/muscular bruises).
answer: Modified Y-shaped Incision: Used for detailed neck dissection in hanging/strangulation.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] In which sequence are body cavities opened in a suspected asphyxial death to avoid Prinsloo-Gordon artefacts? {{c1::Cranial cavity first → Thorax → Neck LAST (bloodless neck dissection)}}.
answer: Newborn Autopsy Sequence (HAT): Head → Abdomen → Thorax.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which organ removal technique is preferred in an HIV-positive or highly infectious cadaver? {{c1::Rokitansky technique (in-situ dissection)}}.
answer: Other Techniques: Virchow (organ-by-organ, M/C), Letulle (en masse), Ghon (3 blocks).

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] Fragmentation of retinal blood vessels (Kevorkian / cattle-trucking sign) appears within what time after death? {{c1::Few minutes to 1 hour}}.
answer: Tache Noire Sclerotica: Appears at 3–6 hours when eyes remain open.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which sample is the MOST RELIABLE for estimating Time Since Death (TSD) in a decomposed body? {{c1::Vitreous humor (rising potassium K⁺ levels)}}.
answer: Advantage: Vitreous humor is anatomically isolated and resists bacterial putrefaction longer than blood.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] According to Casper's dictum, the ratio of rate of putrefaction in Air : Water : Earth is {{c1::1 : 2 : 8}} (Air is fastest, Earth is slowest).
answer: Memory Aid: A body decomposes 2× slower in water and 8× slower in earth compared to air.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which soft tissue organ is the LAST to putrefy in females and males respectively? {{c1::Non-gravid uterus (females) and Prostate (males)}}.
answer: Earliest to Putrefy: Larynx and Trachea. Hard Tissues Last: Bone & Teeth.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] Postmortem caloricity (body remaining warm after death) is seen in all EXCEPT {{c1::severe burns}} (seen in heat stroke, pontine hemorrhage, septicemia, tetanus, and strychnine poisoning).
answer: Mechanism: Excessive antemortem heat generation or hypothalamic failure.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] At what time after death does postmortem lividity (hypostasis) become fixed (blanching becomes negative)? {{c1::6–12 hours}}.
answer: Timeline: Onset 30 mins → Visible 1–4 hrs → Fixed 6–12 hrs.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] In which muscle/organ does rigor mortis appear FIRST internally? {{c1::Myocardium (within 1 hour)}}.
answer: Externally (Nysten's Rule): Eyelids → Neck → Jaw → Face → Thorax → Upper limb → Abdomen → Lower limb → Fingers/toes.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] What is the ideal preservative for viscera in chemical analysis (though avoided in alcohol/formalin/phosphorus poisoning)? {{c1::Rectified spirit}} (most common in India is Saturated NaCl).
answer: Blood Preservative: Sodium fluoride + Potassium oxalate (for alcohol/poisons); EDTA (for DNA).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Why is a soil sample collected around the coffin during exhumation in a suspected arsenic poisoning case? {{c1::To differentiate antemortem poisoning from postmortem imbibition of arsenic from soil}}.
answer: Exhumation Authorization: Magistrate (196 BNSS); no time limit in India.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A body recovered from a river has weeds and grass tightly clenched in the right hand, which cannot be opened easily. What is this phenomenon and its significance? {{c1::Cadaveric spasm; Surest sign of antemortem drowning}}.
answer: Key Fact: Cadaveric spasm has NO primary relaxation and is ALWAYS antemortem.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which tissue is the BEST site for performing the Diatom test in a suspected drowning case with putrefaction? {{c1::Bone marrow (sternum or femur)}}.
answer: Why Bone Marrow: Protected from contamination; silica cell wall of diatoms resists acid digestion and putrefaction.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] At autopsy of a drowning victim, subpleural, pale-red, ill-defined hemorrhagic patches are found on the anterior/lower lung surfaces due to alveolar rupture. Name them: {{c1::Paltauf hemorrhages}}.
answer: Specificity: Paltauf hemorrhages are specific to wet drowning (unlike Tardieu petechial spots which are non-specific).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which autopsy finding is considered the SUREST sign of antemortem hanging? {{c1::Dribbling of saliva from the angle of mouth opposite to the knot}}.
answer: Other Antemortem Hanging Sign: La facie sympathique (ipsilateral open eye + dilated pupil).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A victim of homicidal manual strangulation (throttling) shows coin-shaped fingertip bruises on the neck and an inward fracture of the hyoid greater cornu. What are these called? {{c1::Six-penny bruises and Adduction fracture of hyoid}}.
answer: Contrast: Hanging causes abduction (outward) hyoid fracture, seen mostly > 40 years.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] In Gettler's test for drowning, right heart chloride is significantly higher than left heart chloride (>25% difference). What type of drowning is this? {{c1::Freshwater drowning (hemodilution in left heart)}}.
answer: Saltwater Drowning: Left heart Cl⁻ > Right heart Cl⁻ (hemoconcentration).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] What does 'Washerwoman's hand and feet' signify in a body recovered from water? {{c1::Only the duration/time since immersion (occurs in both antemortem and postmortem immersion)}}.
answer: Timeline: Starts in fingers at 3–4 hrs → whole hand by 24 hrs.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A transverse intimal tear of the carotid artery seen in hanging is called {{c1::Amussat sign}}, and intervertebral disc hemorrhage is called {{c2::Simon's hemorrhage}}.
answer: Judicial Hanging: C2 Hangman's fracture.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] During an altercation, a person is pinned under a heavy iron beam across the chest, presenting at autopsy with a pale chest and deeply cyanosed face with conjunctival petechiae. Name the syndrome: {{c1::Traumatic asphyxia (Perthes syndrome / Masque ecchymotique)}}.
answer: Burking: Homicidal smothering + traumatic asphyxia.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] An intoxicated man eating steak suddenly collapses and dies silently at a restaurant without clutching his throat, mimicking an MI. Diagnosis and mechanism? {{c1::Cafe coronary syndrome; Vagal inhibition of the heart}}.
answer: Conscious Choking First Aid: Heimlich maneuver.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which single bone feature has the HIGHEST accuracy for sex determination? {{c1::Greater sciatic notch of the pelvis}} (Pelvis overall = 95% Krogman's accuracy).
answer: Male vs Female Notch: Deep & narrow in males; Wide & shallow in females.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] An elbow X-ray shows that all 6 ossification centers (CRITOE) have appeared, but none have fused yet. What is the estimated age? {{c1::11 to 16 years}} (Lateral epicondyle appears at 11y; fusion occurs at 16–17y).
answer: CRITOE Ages: C(1), R(5), I(6), T(9), O(9), E(11).

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] Which ossification center is the LAST to fuse in the human skeleton and at what age? {{c1::Medial end of clavicle; 21–22 years}}.
answer: Adult (>18 yrs) Best X-ray: Wrist joint (fusion of lower end of radius at 18–19 yrs).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Under Gustafson's method for adult dental age estimation (>25 yrs), which criterion is the MOST RELIABLE? {{c1::Transparency of root}} (followed by secondary dentin).
answer: Mnemonic APSRTC: Attrition, Paradentosis, Secondary dentin, Root resorption, Transparency of root, Cementum apposition.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] What is the MOST COMMON fingerprint pattern (Galton's system), and how many cores and deltas does it have? {{c1::Loop pattern (~65%); 1 core and 1 delta}}.
answer: Whorl: 1 core, 2 deltas. Arch: 0 core, 0 delta. Comparison: Can differentiate identical twins!

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] Which identification method can definitively differentiate between monozygotic (identical) twins? {{c1::Dactylography (fingerprinting)}}.
answer: Note: Identical twins share the same DNA profile, but their dermal ridge patterns are unique.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A femur is found measuring 45 cm on a Hepburn osteometric board. Using the multiplication factor (FeTHUR), what is the estimated stature? {{c1::45 × 3.7 = 166.5 cm}}.
answer: FeTHUR Factors: Femur 3.7, Tibia 4.5, Humerus 5.3, Ulna 6.1, Radius 6.5.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Shovel-shaped incisors and taurodontism are dental characteristics of which race? {{c1::Mongoloid race (Mnemonic PASTE)}}.
answer: Caucasoid: Carabelli's cusp.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] Inquest in a case of dowry death (within 7 years of marriage) or custodial death is mandatorily conducted by {{c1::Magistrate (Section 196 BNSS)}}.
answer: 3 Mandatory Magistrate Inquest Situations: Custodial death/rape, Dowry death, Exhumation.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A surgeon leaves a gauze sponge inside the abdomen during laparotomy. Which legal doctrine applies and who bears the burden of proof? {{c1::Res ipsa loquitur ('Fact speaks for itself'); Burden shifts to the doctor}}.
answer: Scope: Applies to both civil and criminal negligence; no expert witness testimony is required.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which WMA Declaration governs guidelines on {{c1::Torture}} vs {{c2::Human Experimentation}} vs {{c3::Therapeutic Abortion}}? {{c1::Tokyo}}, {{c2::Helsinki}}, and {{c3::Oslo}} respectively.
answer: Quick List: Geneva (Ethics), Sydney (Death), Venice (Terminal illness), Lisbon (Patient rights), Malta (Hunger strike), Washington (Biological weapons).

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] Under the MTP (Amendment) Act 2021, termination between 20–24 weeks requires the opinion of {{c1::2 registered medical practitioners}}, and beyond 24 weeks requires a {{c2::Medical Board}} (only for substantial fetal anomaly).
answer: Record Preservation: 5 years; monthly report to District CMO.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A 1-year-old child presents with bilateral posterior rib 'string-of-beads' callus fractures of varying ages and a torn lower lip frenulum. Diagnosis? {{c1::Battered Baby Syndrome (Caffey-Kempe syndrome / Child Abuse)}}.
answer: Classic Clue: Multiple fractures/bruises at different stages of healing + discrepancy in history.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Which confirmatory microchemical test for blood stains produces {{c1::pink feathery hemochromogen crystals}}? {{c1::Takayama test}} (Teichmann gives brown rhombic hemin crystals).
answer: Presumptive Tests: Benzidine (blue), Kastle-Meyer/Phenolphthalein (pink), Luminol (washed stains).

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] Which seminal stain test detects spermine from prostatic secretions by forming yellow needle-shaped crystals? {{c1::Barberio's test (Spermine picrate crystals)}}.
answer: Florence Test: Dark brown rhombic choline iodide crystals. Confirmatory: ≥ 1 intact spermatozoon.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Microscopic examination of a hair strand shows a fragmented narrow medulla with a medullary index of 0.18 (< 0.3). This is {{c1::Human hair}} (Animal hair has medullary index > 0.5).
answer: Animal Hair: Wide, continuous medulla.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] Under Section {{c1::116 BNS}}, hurt causing severe bodily pain or inability to follow ordinary pursuits for {{c2::15 days}} (updated from 20 days in IPC 320) is classified as {{c3::Grievous Hurt}}.
answer: Other New BNS Sections: 63 (Rape), 103 (Murder), 106(1) (Medical negligence death), 124 (Vitriolage).

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] Under THOA 1994 (2014), who is NEVER allowed to be a member of the 4-member brainstem death certification board? {{c1::The transplant surgeon}}.
answer: Testing Interval: Two examinations 6 hours apart.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A doctor receives a summons from a Sessions (Criminal) Court and a Civil Court for the same date and time. Which court must the doctor attend first? {{c1::Sessions (Criminal) Court}} (Criminal > Civil).
answer: Equal Courts: Attend the one that summoned first. Hierarchy: Higher > Lower court.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A patient with chronic arsenic poisoning presents with transverse white bands across the fingernails and dappled pigmentation on the palms. Name these findings: {{c1::Aldrich-Mees lines and Raindrop pigmentation}}.
answer: Differential: Mees lines + GBS-like neuropathy also occur in Thallium, but Thallium uniquely causes madarosis.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] A battery-factory worker presents with wrist drop, abdominal colic, microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling, and a blue-black gingival line. Which enzyme inhibition causes basophilic stippling? {{c1::5'-pyrimidine nucleotidase}}.
answer: Gingival Line: Burtonian line. Screening Test: Urinary ALA ↑↑.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A match-factory worker develops painful osteonecrosis of the mandible with multiple garlicky discharging sinuses. Diagnosis & toxin? {{c1::Phossy jaw; White phosphorus}}.
answer: Acute White Phosphorus: Luminescent vomitus/stool ('Smoky stool syndrome') → Asymptomatic stage → Hepatic failure.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A traveler is given prasad by a stranger and develops 'hot as a hare, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter' (muttering delirium, dilated pupils). Antidote of choice? {{c1::Physostigmine (Datura poisoning)}}.
answer: Trap: Do NOT use Neostigmine (does not cross BBB to reverse central anticholinergic delirium).

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] An international passenger presents with multiple cylindrical packets on abdominal X-ray (Body Packer Syndrome) and is asymptomatic. Management? {{c1::Whole bowel irrigation with Polyethylene Glycol (PEG)}}.
answer: If Cocaine Packet Ruptures: Emergency surgery + Amyl nitrite / Benzodiazepines.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A patient with severe backward arching of the spine (opisthotonus) and risus sardonicus remains fully conscious between convulsions. Toxin & neurotransmitter blocked? {{c1::Strychnine (Strychnos nux vomica); Blocks Glycine}}.
answer: Differentiate from Tetanus: Strychnine has rapid onset, triggers on slight stimulus, and muscles relax completely between spasms.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A family develops bilateral pitting pedal edema, diarrhea, and glaucoma after consuming adulterated mustard oil. Causative plant & toxin? {{c1::Argemone mexicana; Sanguinarine (Epidemic Dropsy)}}.
answer: Confirmatory Test: Paper chromatography / Nitric acid test on oil.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] A snakebite victim develops early bilateral ptosis and progressive descending paralysis. Which bedside test monitors impending respiratory failure? {{c1::Single Breath Count Test (Elapidae / Cobra-Krait bite)}}.
answer: Treatment: Polyvalent ASV + IV Neostigmine with Atropine (reverses neuromuscular block in Cobra bite).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A farmer bitten by a snake with 3 rows of diamond-shaped spots develops gum bleeding and unclotted blood at 20 minutes (20-min WBCT). Identify the snake: {{c1::Russell's viper (Daboia russeli — Viperidae)}}.
answer: Venom Type: Hemotoxic (causes DIC, spontaneous bleeding, acute kidney injury).

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A child stung by an Indian Red Scorpion develops hypertension, tachycardia, cold extremities, and pulmonary edema (autonomic storm). Drug of choice? {{c1::Prazosin (alpha-1 blocker)}}.
answer: Mechanism: Prazosin reverses intense alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and prevents cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

question: [PYQ — INI-CET] A patient treated for organophosphorus poisoning recovers from acute cholinergic crisis, then develops proximal limb weakness and cranial nerve palsies on Day 3. Diagnosis & management? {{c1::Intermediate syndrome (1–4 days); Supportive / mechanical ventilation}}.
answer: Delayed Neuropathy (1–4 weeks): Distal neuropathy due to Neuropathy Target Esterase (NTE) inhibition.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] In suspected aluminium phosphide (Celphos) poisoning, filter paper impregnated with {{c1::silver nitrate}} turns {{c2::black}} due to liberated {{c3::phosphine gas}}.
answer: Management: No specific antidote; supportive care + MgSO₄ for arrhythmias.

question: [PYQ — NEET PG] A man found dead in a closed garage with a running car engine has cherry-red postmortem lividity and bilateral symmetrical necrosis of the {{c1::lenticular nucleus (globus pallidus)}}. Toxin? {{c2::Carbon monoxide (CO)}}.
